title: The painful price of four years of RBA rate rises
full_text:
The monthly cost of repaying a typical new home loan has more than doubled in just 4½ years, as homeowners brace for another rate rise.
Analysis by The Australian shows an average new 30-year mortgage today costs borrowers $4819 a month, compared with $2354 in April 2022, when interest rates started increasing.
While home prices have begun falling, they are still higher than they were four years ago, meaning the average owner-occupier mortgage size sits at $731,000, compared to $603,000 in 2022, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.
But the biggest culprit to higher repayment costs – accounting for almost three-quarters of the rise – is the RBA’s cash rate, which has surged from 0.1 per cent to 4.6 per cent. That has lifted mortgage interest rates from 2.41 per cent to 6.91 per cent, and they are likely to push even higher in November.
The odds of another RBA rate rise on Melbourne Cup Day increased after headline inflation hit 4.3 per cent on Wednesday. A rise would mean repayment costs will have surged 110 per cent since 2022, more than five times the pace of Australia’s average wages growth over four years.
Global X ETFs senior investment strategist Marc Jocum said a further rise was looking increasingly difficult to avoid.
“This is an ugly number for the RBA and significantly strengthens the case for another rate hike next week,” he said.
As some mortgage brokers say people’s home-loan pain has never been worse, financial markets are forecasting an 80 per cent chance of another RBA rate rise by December, and the government’s controversial budget tax changes for property investors have failed to achieve their aim of encouraging more first-home buyers into the market.
Credit agency Equifax reports that first-home buyer demand was down 22.1 per cent for the year to September 30, with the biggest falls in Queensland, the ACT and NSW.
Equifax chief solution officer Kevin James said the buyer decline had continued to deepen, and younger buyers were facing compounding pressures despite recent dips in property values.
“Combined with strict serviceability testing, high interest rates and broader cost-of-living inflation are eroding confidence,” Mr James said.
Canstar director of data insights Sally Tindall said new borrowers had suffered a “triple whammy” of rising interest rates, rising rents that made saving for a deposit more difficult and, until recently, rising property prices “that for many years were defying gravity”.
“Property prices in theory should start to cool when interest rates rise, but they just hadn’t up until recently, and part of that was the federal government’s tax changes in addition to rising rates,” Ms Tindall said.
She said the government’s property tax changes had frozen buying activity. “And the market hasn’t unfrozen yet, because we’ve got an environment where we’re just not sure where prices are going to land as a result of these tax changes, and we’re not sure where interest rates will land with an RBA that is repeatedly telling us that it will do what it takes in order to get inflation under control,” she said.
“Yes, property prices are falling, but are they falling by more than what people’s borrowing capacity is dropping by? In some cases, yes we will see that, but in other markets we just don’t know yet.
“Every time the RBA fires up a rate rise it reduces someone’s maximum homebuying budget for an average income earner by $10,000 or $12,000.
“That’s not a huge hit in isolation, but when you add up four already this year and a potential fifth, you are talking about significant drops.” Beyond Bank chief member banking officer Sophie Scott-Young said higher interest rates and reduced demand from property investors meant real estate was “becoming a buyers’ market again”. However, Ms Scott-Young said buyers should focus on making sure their home loan was sustainable over the longer term.
“There’s no doubt affordability remains a challenge for people looking to enter the property market,” she said.
Ms Scott-Young said government deposit assistance schemes were still delivering “some really positive outcomes” for people wanting to become homeowners.
However, others have noted the unfortunate timing of the government introducing more generous homebuyer incentives in late 2025, only to then smash the property market with a tax overhaul announced in May 2026.
Ms Tindall said the home guarantee scheme had helped push people into the market “but at this point in time I think we have to stop and think about whether that strategically has been a great idea”.
More first-home buyers were facing negative equity, and some were there already, she said.
“It pushes people to take on bigger debts, and that’s not sustainable.”
